countries.name: Australia
countries.summary: Australia is in the southern hemisphere, so summer is December to February and winter June to August, and its size means the seasons run in opposite directions. The southern half (Sydney, Melbourne, Adelaide, Perth, Tasmania) is best in spring (September–November) and autumn (March–May), with hot summers that bring bushfire risk and cool, damp winters. The tropical north (Cairns, the Great Barrier Reef, Darwin, Kakadu, the Kimberley) has a dry season from May to October and a hot wet season from November to April with cyclones, flooded roads and box jellyfish. The Red Centre around Uluru is best in the mild winter, as summer days pass 36 °C. Australian school holidays (Christmas to late January, and two weeks around Easter) fill beaches, campsites and flights.

regions.name: Sydney & New South Wales
regions.description: Sydney and its beaches (Bondi, Manly), the Blue Mountains, Byron Bay, the Hunter Valley, Port Stephens, Jervis Bay, Canberra and the Snowy Mountains ski fields (Thredbo, Perisher).

best.why: Spring: sunny 20–24 °C days, jacarandas flowering in November, clear Blue Mountains walks and uncrowded beaches before the summer holidays.
Autumn: settled 20–25 °C weather, the sea still 22–23 °C in March, Hunter Valley harvest and school holidays over.

worst.why: Coolest months: 16–17 °C days and 8 °C nights, the sea is too cold for most swimmers and the Blue Mountains are frosty (still fine for city sightseeing, and the Snowy Mountains ski season is on).

shoulder.why: Hot, humid beach season (26 °C, heatwaves above 35 °C), with New Year's Eve fireworks and peak summer-holiday prices and crowds.
Cooling down; Vivid Sydney light festival from late May.
Late winter: sunny, dry days warming up, whales migrating along the coast.

risks.note: Bushfires in the Blue Mountains and on the coast; smoke can blanket Sydney and parks close on catastrophic fire-danger days.
Western Sydney heatwaves above 40 °C.
East-coast lows bring days of torrential rain, flooding and dangerous surf.

recurringHolidays.name: New Year's Eve in Sydney
recurringHolidays.effect: Harbour fireworks: harbour-view hotels and restaurants triple their prices and book out months ahead.

recurringHolidays.name: Vivid Sydney
recurringHolidays.effect: Light installations and concerts around the harbour; central hotels fill.

recurringHolidays.name: Australian summer school holidays
recurringHolidays.effect: Beach towns, campsites, ferries and domestic flights book out and prices peak, especially between Christmas and New Year.

recurringHolidays.name: Easter and the autumn school holidays
recurringHolidays.approx: Easter long weekend plus about two weeks (varies by state)
recurringHolidays.effect: Coastal and national-park accommodation fills with families and airfares rise.

prices.notes: Sydney is Australia's most expensive city; harbour-view rooms around New Year's Eve cost several times the usual rate. Opal-card public transport and free beaches keep daily costs down.

regions.name: Melbourne & Victoria
regions.description: Melbourne, the Great Ocean Road and Twelve Apostles, the Yarra Valley, Mornington Peninsula, Phillip Island, the Grampians, Wilsons Promontory and the Victorian Alps ski resorts (Mount Buller, Falls Creek, Mount Hotham).

best.why: Late summer and autumn: the most settled weather of the year (20–26 °C), the Grand Prix and the food and wine festival in March, and vineyards turning gold.
Late spring: 20–24 °C days, gardens in flower and the Spring Racing Carnival with the Melbourne Cup in early November.

worst.why: Cold, grey and windy winter: 14 °C days, drizzle and early dusk on the Great Ocean Road (but it is the Victorian Alps' ski season).

shoulder.why: Hot, changeable summer with 40 °C heatwaves and sudden cool changes, school-holiday crowds on the Great Ocean Road and the Australian Open in late January.
Crisp autumn days, cooling quickly.
Changeable spring, often windy and showery; AFL Grand Final in late September.

risks.note: Bushfires in the Grampians, the Otways and Gippsland; check VicEmergency before driving.
Heatwaves above 40 °C, usually broken by a sudden 'cool change'.
Winter gales and big swells on the Great Ocean Road coast.

recurringHolidays.name: Australian Open
recurringHolidays.effect: Tennis crowds fill central Melbourne hotels and prices jump.

recurringHolidays.name: Melbourne Cup
recurringHolidays.effect: A public holiday in Melbourne and the peak of the Spring Racing Carnival; hotels book out.

recurringHolidays.name: Australian summer school holidays
recurringHolidays.effect: Beach towns, campsites, ferries and domestic flights book out and prices peak, especially between Christmas and New Year.

recurringHolidays.name: Easter and the autumn school holidays
recurringHolidays.approx: Easter long weekend plus about two weeks (varies by state)
recurringHolidays.effect: Coastal and national-park accommodation fills with families and airfares rise.

prices.notes: Melbourne is slightly cheaper than Sydney, with free trams in the city centre. Ski-resort lodging on the mountains is expensive in July and on weekends.

regions.name: Queensland & the Great Barrier Reef
regions.description: Brisbane, the Gold Coast, the Sunshine Coast and Noosa, K'gari (Fraser Island), the Whitsundays, Cairns, Port Douglas, the Great Barrier Reef and the Daintree rainforest; climate figures are for Cairns in the tropical north.

best.why: Dry season: sunny 26–29 °C days, low humidity, calm seas, stinger-free water in the far north from June to September and the best reef visibility from August.

worst.why: Tropical wet season in the north: heavy rain, cyclones, flooded roads in the Daintree and box jellyfish (stingers) in the sea, with humid storms in Brisbane and school-holiday crowds on the Gold Coast.

shoulder.why: The rains ease and the country is green; stinger suits are still needed and some Daintree roads are only just reopening.
Hot and humid with the first storms; coral spawning on the reef and stinger season starts.

risks.note: Tropical cyclones can close islands, reef trips and airports in north Queensland.
Monsoon rain cuts the Bruce Highway and Daintree roads.
Box and Irukandji jellyfish: swim only in netted areas or wear a stinger suit north of Gladstone.

recurringHolidays.name: Australian summer school holidays
recurringHolidays.effect: Beach towns, campsites, ferries and domestic flights book out and prices peak, especially between Christmas and New Year.

recurringHolidays.name: Easter and the autumn school holidays
recurringHolidays.approx: Easter long weekend plus about two weeks (varies by state)
recurringHolidays.effect: Coastal and national-park accommodation fills with families and airfares rise.

prices.notes: A day trip to the outer reef costs about $180–280 with snorkelling, more with dives. Island resorts in the Whitsundays are expensive; Airlie Beach and Cairns have plenty of cheap hostels.

regions.name: Uluru & the Red Centre
regions.description: Uluru and Kata Tjuta, Alice Springs, Kings Canyon (Watarrka) and the West MacDonnell Ranges with the Larapinta Trail.

best.why: Winter in the desert: sunny 20–28 °C days, clear starry nights and comfortable conditions for the Uluru base walk, Kings Canyon rim and the Larapinta Trail (nights can drop near 0 °C).

worst.why: Searing summer: 36–40 °C days, plagues of flies and storms; the Kings Canyon rim walk and Uluru base walk close from 9am on hot days.

shoulder.why: Heat easing, wildflowers after summer rain, Easter crowds at Uluru.
Hot afternoons above 30 °C; start walks at dawn.

risks.note: Days above 40 °C; carry plenty of water and walk only in the early morning.
Grass fires can close roads in the MacDonnell Ranges.

recurringHolidays.name: Australian summer school holidays
recurringHolidays.effect: Beach towns, campsites, ferries and domestic flights book out and prices peak, especially between Christmas and New Year.

recurringHolidays.name: Easter and the autumn school holidays
recurringHolidays.approx: Easter long weekend plus about two weeks (varies by state)
recurringHolidays.effect: Coastal and national-park accommodation fills with families and airfares rise.

prices.notes: Ayers Rock Resort has a near-monopoly on Uluru beds, so rooms cost far more than elsewhere; camping and the hostel are the budget options. Park passes are about A$38 for three days.

regions.name: Darwin, Kakadu & the Kimberley
regions.description: Darwin, Kakadu and Litchfield national parks, Katherine (Nitmiluk) Gorge, Broome and Cable Beach, the Kimberley with the Gibb River Road and Purnululu (Bungle Bungles).

best.why: Dry season: sunny 31 °C days, low humidity, roads and swimming holes open in Kakadu and Litchfield, the Gibb River Road passable and Darwin's sunset markets running.

worst.why: The wet: monsoon downpours, cyclones, flooded roads and closed parks (Jim Jim Falls, the Gibb River Road and Purnululu shut), plus box jellyfish in the sea.

shoulder.why: End of the wet: waterfalls thunder and scenic flights are spectacular, but many Kakadu and Kimberley roads stay closed until May or June.
The 'build-up': 35 °C and very humid, with afternoon storms building.

risks.note: Tropical cyclones hit Darwin and the Kimberley coast.
Wet-season flooding closes Kakadu's unsealed roads, the Gibb River Road and Purnululu.
Box jellyfish (and saltwater crocodiles all year) make the sea unsafe for swimming.

recurringHolidays.name: Australian summer school holidays
recurringHolidays.effect: Beach towns, campsites, ferries and domestic flights book out and prices peak, especially between Christmas and New Year.

recurringHolidays.name: Easter and the autumn school holidays
recurringHolidays.approx: Easter long weekend plus about two weeks (varies by state)
recurringHolidays.effect: Coastal and national-park accommodation fills with families and airfares rise.

prices.notes: Kakadu requires a park pass (about A$40). A 4WD is needed for the Gibb River Road and many Kakadu sites; Broome's resorts are pricey in the dry season.

regions.name: Perth & Western Australia
regions.description: Perth and Fremantle, Rottnest Island, Margaret River, the Pinnacles, Kalbarri, Shark Bay (Monkey Mia), Ningaloo Reef and Exmouth, Esperance and Karijini.

best.why: Spring: 22–27 °C sunshine, wildflowers carpeting the south-west and the Midwest, and humpback whales off Exmouth and Augusta.
Late summer and autumn: dry, warm days, a 23 °C sea, the Margaret River harvest, and whale sharks arriving at Ningaloo from March.

worst.why: Perth's wettest months: 18 °C days and frequent cold fronts, rough Rottnest crossings and a chilly sea (the dry north around Ningaloo is pleasant, though).

shoulder.why: Hot (30–40 °C), dry beach season with school-holiday crowds and bushfire risk; the 'Fremantle Doctor' sea breeze cools afternoons.
Cooling down, first winter rains; whale sharks still at Ningaloo.
Wildflower season beginning, showers easing.

risks.note: Perth heatwaves above 40 °C; inland and the Pilbara reach 45 °C.
Bushfires in the hills and the south-west forests.
Cyclones strike the Pilbara and Ningaloo coast.

recurringHolidays.name: Australian summer school holidays
recurringHolidays.effect: Beach towns, campsites, ferries and domestic flights book out and prices peak, especially between Christmas and New Year.

recurringHolidays.name: Easter and the autumn school holidays
recurringHolidays.approx: Easter long weekend plus about two weeks (varies by state)
recurringHolidays.effect: Coastal and national-park accommodation fills with families and airfares rise.

prices.notes: Distances are vast: Perth to Exmouth is 1,250 km, so many people fly. A swim with whale sharks costs about A$500.

regions.name: Adelaide & South Australia
regions.description: Adelaide and Glenelg, the Barossa, Clare and McLaren Vale wine regions, the Adelaide Hills (Hahndorf), Kangaroo Island, the Flinders Ranges and Coober Pedy.

best.why: Late summer and autumn: warm, dry 22–28 °C days, the Adelaide Fringe and festival season in March, the Barossa vintage and good Kangaroo Island wildlife viewing.
Spring: green hills, wildflowers in the Flinders Ranges and pleasant 20–25 °C days before the summer heat.

worst.why: Coolest and wettest months: 15 °C days, rain and rough Kangaroo Island ferry crossings (still good for the outback Flinders Ranges).

shoulder.why: Hot, dry summer with 40 °C heatwaves and high bushfire danger; Tour Down Under cycling in January.
Autumn colours in the Adelaide Hills, cooling quickly.
Late winter warming up; whales at Victor Harbor.

risks.note: Adelaide heatwaves above 40 °C; the outback is hotter still.
Bushfires in the Adelaide Hills and on Kangaroo Island.

recurringHolidays.name: Adelaide Fringe and Festival
recurringHolidays.effect: The world's second-largest fringe festival; Adelaide hotels fill and prices rise.

recurringHolidays.name: Australian summer school holidays
recurringHolidays.effect: Beach towns, campsites, ferries and domestic flights book out and prices peak, especially between Christmas and New Year.

recurringHolidays.name: Easter and the autumn school holidays
recurringHolidays.approx: Easter long weekend plus about two weeks (varies by state)
recurringHolidays.effect: Coastal and national-park accommodation fills with families and airfares rise.

prices.notes: Adelaide is one of Australia's cheaper big cities. Wine tastings at Barossa cellar doors are often free or a few dollars.

regions.name: Tasmania
regions.description: Hobart and MONA, Bruny Island, Port Arthur, Freycinet and Wineglass Bay, the Bay of Fires, Cradle Mountain and the Overland Track, Launceston and Strahan.

best.why: Summer and early autumn: mild 20–23 °C days with long evenings, open hiking trails at Cradle Mountain and Freycinet, and the Taste of Tasmania food festival over New Year.

worst.why: Cold, wet winter: 12 °C days, snow and closed tracks at Cradle Mountain and short days (though Hobart's Dark Mofo festival in June is worth the chill).

shoulder.why: Crisp autumn days and the golden 'turning of the fagus' at Cradle Mountain; frosty nights.
Spring: changeable, windy weather, with gardens and wildflowers coming out.

risks.note: Bushfires in the forests and highlands can close national parks.
Snow and ice on highland roads and the Overland Track.

recurringHolidays.name: Dark Mofo
recurringHolidays.effect: Hobart's midwinter arts festival around the solstice; hotels fill and prices jump.

recurringHolidays.name: Taste of Tasmania
recurringHolidays.effect: Hobart's waterfront food festival during peak summer season.

recurringHolidays.name: Australian summer school holidays
recurringHolidays.effect: Beach towns, campsites, ferries and domestic flights book out and prices peak, especially between Christmas and New Year.

recurringHolidays.name: Easter and the autumn school holidays
recurringHolidays.approx: Easter long weekend plus about two weeks (varies by state)
recurringHolidays.effect: Coastal and national-park accommodation fills with families and airfares rise.

prices.notes: Hire a car: public transport barely reaches the national parks. The Overland Track costs about A$285 in the booked season (October–May).

countries.name: Cook Islands
countries.summary: The Cook Islands, a self-governing territory in free association with New Zealand, have a warm, sunny dry season from May to October with 24–26 °C days, lower humidity and the best snorkelling in Aitutaki's lagoon. November to April is hotter, more humid and wetter, with a cyclone risk that peaks from January to March. New Zealand school holidays (July, late September–October and Christmas) bring families to Rarotonga's resorts. Humpback whales pass from July to October.
countries.splitReason: Rarotonga and Aitutaki, where nearly all visitors stay, share one tropical climate and season.

regions.name: Whole country
regions.description: Rarotonga (Avarua, Muri Lagoon, the Cross-Island Track), Aitutaki and its lagoon, Atiu and Mangaia.

best.why: Dry season: sunny 24–26 °C days, low humidity, clear lagoons for snorkelling and humpback whales offshore from July.

worst.why: Hot, humid wet season with heavy showers and the main cyclone risk.

shoulder.why: Warmer and more humid, with occasional heavy showers; busy around Christmas.
Rains easing; quiet and good value.

risks.note: Tropical cyclones, most likely January to March.

recurringHolidays.name: Te Maeva Nui
recurringHolidays.effect: The week-long constitution celebrations with dance and song competitions on Rarotonga; accommodation fills.

recurringHolidays.name: New Zealand winter school holidays
recurringHolidays.effect: Rarotonga's family resorts fill and prices rise.

prices.notes: Prices are in New Zealand dollars and are similar to New Zealand's. Aitutaki is pricier than Rarotonga; a lagoon cruise costs about $100.

countries.name: Fiji
countries.summary: Fiji is warm all year (26–31 °C), so the seasons are about rain and cyclones. The drier, slightly cooler season from May to October has sunny days, lower humidity and the clearest water for diving and snorkelling, and is the peak time for visitors. November to April is the wet season, with heavy showers, high humidity and a cyclone risk that peaks from January to March. Australian and New Zealand school holidays (July, late September and Christmas) fill the family resorts on Denarau, the Mamanucas and the Coral Coast.
countries.splitReason: Viti Levu, Vanua Levu and the outer island groups share the same tropical wet and dry calendar; the western side (Nadi, the Mamanucas, the Yasawas) is simply drier than Suva.

regions.name: Whole country
regions.description: Nadi and Denarau, the Mamanuca and Yasawa islands, the Coral Coast, Pacific Harbour and Beqa, Suva, Taveuni, Savusavu and Kadavu.

best.why: Dry season: sunny 28–29 °C days, low humidity, calm lagoons and the best visibility for diving the soft corals of Rainbow Reef and Beqa.

worst.why: Height of the wet season: heavy downpours, steamy 31 °C days and the main cyclone risk, which can cancel island transfers.

shoulder.why: Hot and increasingly humid, with afternoon showers and the start of cyclone season.
Rains tailing off, lush and quieter, with good resort deals.

risks.note: Tropical cyclones, most likely January to March, can close ports and airports.
Flash floods on Viti Levu, especially around Nadi and Ba.

recurringHolidays.name: Australian and New Zealand winter school holidays
recurringHolidays.effect: Family resorts in Denarau, the Mamanucas and the Coral Coast fill and prices rise.

recurringHolidays.name: Christmas and New Year
recurringHolidays.effect: Peak season for Australian and New Zealand families; resorts book out.

recurringHolidays.name: Diwali
recurringHolidays.effect: A public holiday celebrated by Indo-Fijians with lights and sweets; some shops close.

prices.notes: Island resorts in the Mamanucas and Yasawas are mostly full-board and pricey; the Yasawa Flyer ferry and backpacker resorts are the budget route. Prices are usually quoted in Fijian dollars.

countries.name: Guam
countries.summary: Guam, a US territory, is hot and humid all year at around 30 °C. The dry season from December to May has trade winds, sunshine and calm seas on the Tumon Bay beaches. July to November is the rainy season and the peak of the typhoon season, although strong typhoons can strike at any time of year. Japanese, Korean and Taiwanese holidays such as Golden Week and New Year bring surges of visitors to Tumon.
countries.splitReason: Guam is a single island 50 km long with one tropical climate.

regions.name: Whole country
regions.description: Tumon Bay's beaches and hotels, Hagåtña, Two Lovers Point, Ritidian Point, the Inarajan pools, Cocos Island and the wartime sites of the War in the Pacific National Historical Park.

best.why: Dry season: sunny 29–30 °C days, steady trade winds and calm, clear water for snorkelling in Tumon Bay.

worst.why: Rainy season and the height of the typhoon season, with heavy showers, high humidity and rough seas.

shoulder.why: Hot and increasingly humid as the rains begin.
Rain and typhoon risk tailing off.

risks.note: Super typhoons can hit Guam (Mawar in May 2023 showed they can come early).
An active seismic zone.

recurringHolidays.name: Japanese Golden Week
recurringHolidays.effect: Tumon Bay hotels fill with Japanese visitors and room rates jump.

recurringHolidays.name: Japanese and Korean New Year holidays
recurringHolidays.effect: Peak season for East Asian visitors; hotels book out and prices peak.

prices.notes: The US dollar is the currency and prices are close to mainland US resort levels. A car is needed to get beyond Tumon.

countries.name: Kiribati
countries.summary: Kiribati straddles the equator, so it is hot (around 31 °C) and humid all year with little temperature change. Rain varies more than heat: on Tarawa the driest months are usually September to November and the wettest January to April, but El Niño years can bring months of heavy rain while La Niña years bring drought. Kiritimati (Christmas Island), far to the east, is drier and is visited mainly for bonefishing and birdwatching. Flights are few, so plan around the schedule rather than the weather.
countries.splitReason: The atolls are tiny and low with an equatorial climate; the differences between Tarawa and Kiritimati are in rainfall amounts rather than timing.

regions.name: Whole country
regions.description: South and North Tarawa (with the Second World War sites at Betio), the outer Gilbert atolls such as Abaiang and Abemama, and Kiritimati in the Line Islands.

best.why: The driest months on Tarawa: steady easterly trade winds, more sunshine and calmer lagoon conditions.

worst.why: Wetter season with squalls and westerly winds, and king tides that flood low-lying parts of South Tarawa.

shoulder.why: Showers easing, hot and humid.
Rain becoming more frequent.

risks.note: King tides and swells wash over the low atolls.
El Niño years bring months of heavy rain.

recurringHolidays.name: Independence Day
recurringHolidays.effect: A week of celebrations, sports and dancing on Tarawa; offices close.

prices.notes: Prices are in Australian dollars. Accommodation is limited to a handful of simple hotels and guesthouses; Kiritimati fishing lodges are sold as week-long packages.

countries.name: Marshall Islands
countries.summary: The Marshall Islands are low coral atolls north of the equator, hot (around 30 °C) and humid all year. The drier trade-wind season runs from December to April, with steady north-east winds, more sunshine and the calmest diving conditions. The rest of the year is wetter, with the heaviest rain from August to November, when tropical storms and typhoons form nearby. King tides in winter can flood parts of Majuro.
countries.splitReason: Majuro, Kwajalein and the outer atolls share one tropical climate, with the northern atolls simply drier.

regions.name: Whole country
regions.description: Majuro atoll, Kwajalein and Ebeye, the outer atolls such as Arno and Mili, and Bikini Atoll's sunken fleet.

best.why: Dry trade-wind season: more sunshine, less rain and the best visibility for diving the lagoons and wrecks.

worst.why: Wettest months, with frequent squalls and tropical storms or typhoons forming nearby.

shoulder.why: Rain increasing and winds lighter.
Trade winds returning and the rains easing.

risks.note: Tropical storms and typhoons form in the area, though direct hits are uncommon.
King tides and swells wash over Majuro's low-lying roads.

prices.notes: The US dollar is the currency. Bikini Atoll dive trips run only occasionally and are very expensive; Majuro hotels are basic.

countries.name: Micronesia
countries.summary: The Federated States of Micronesia (Yap, Chuuk, Pohnpei and Kosrae) are hot and humid all year at around 30 °C. The drier season runs from about January to April, with trade winds and calmer seas, and is the best time for diving Chuuk Lagoon's wartime wrecks and Yap's manta rays. From July to November it is wetter and typhoons form in the area, with Yap the state most exposed. Pohnpei and Kosrae are among the rainiest places on Earth, with rain in every month.
countries.splitReason: The four island states share the same western-Pacific seasons, with the dry season and typhoon season falling at the same time; Pohnpei and Kosrae are simply wetter.

regions.name: Whole country
regions.description: Chuuk Lagoon and its wartime wrecks, Pohnpei (Kolonia and the ruins of Nan Madol), Yap with its stone money and manta rays, and Kosrae; climate figures are for Chuuk.

best.why: Drier trade-wind season: calmer seas, better visibility in Chuuk Lagoon and manta-ray mating season at Yap.

worst.why: Wettest months and the peak of the typhoon season, with rough seas and cancelled flights.

shoulder.why: Rains increasing, diving still good.
Trade winds returning, with lingering storms.

risks.note: Typhoons form in the area and Yap is the most exposed state.
Pohnpei and Kosrae get 5 m of rain or more a year.

recurringHolidays.name: Yap Day
recurringHolidays.effect: Yap's traditional dance festival; the island's few hotels book up.

prices.notes: The US dollar is the currency. Diving is the main cost: Chuuk Lagoon wreck dives cost about $150–200 for two tanks, and liveaboards run in the dry season.

countries.name: Nauru
countries.summary: Nauru is a single small island just south of the equator, hot (around 31 °C) and humid all year. It has a wetter westerly season from about December to February and a drier trade-wind season from May to October, though rainfall swings widely between El Niño years (very wet) and La Niña years (drought). There are few visitors, and visas and the limited flights matter more than the weather. The coastal ring road takes about half an hour to drive.
countries.splitReason: Nauru is a single island of 21 km² with one climate.

regions.name: Whole country
regions.description: Yaren, Anibare Bay, Buada Lagoon, the phosphate-mined interior (Topside) and the wartime guns on Command Ridge.

best.why: Trade-wind season: steady breezes, more sunshine and less rain, with calmer water at Anibare Bay.

worst.why: Westerly season: heavier squalls, higher humidity and rough seas on the western reef.

shoulder.why: Rains easing.
Showers increasing.

risks.note: Westerly squalls bring heavy downpours.
Westerly swells make swimming over the reef dangerous.

prices.notes: Prices are in Australian dollars, and there are only two hotels. Visas must be arranged before arrival and can take weeks.

countries.name: New Zealand
countries.summary: New Zealand is in the southern hemisphere, so summer is December to February. Late summer and early autumn (February to April) is the best overall time, with the most settled weather, the warmest sea and the school holidays over; November and early December are a good spring alternative. Christmas to the end of January is peak season, when New Zealanders take their summer holidays and campsites, Great Walk huts and ferries book out. Winter (June to September) is wet and windy in the North Island but brings the ski season to Queenstown, Wānaka and Mount Ruapehu. The west coast of the South Island (Fiordland, the glaciers) is very wet in every month.

regions.name: North Island
regions.description: Auckland and Waiheke, the Bay of Islands, the Coromandel, Rotorua, Taupō, Tongariro National Park and the Alpine Crossing, Waitomo, Hobbiton, Napier and Hawke's Bay, and Wellington.

best.why: Late summer: settled 23–25 °C days, the warmest sea of the year (21 °C), good Tongariro Crossing conditions and the school-holiday crowds gone.
Late spring: long, mild 20–22 °C days, green countryside and quieter roads before Christmas.

worst.why: Wet, windy winter: 15 °C days, frequent rain in Auckland and snow and ice making the Tongariro Crossing a guided alpine trip (Mount Ruapehu's ski fields open, though).

shoulder.why: Peak summer holidays: warm and sunny but campsites, beaches and the Bay of Islands are packed and prices peak.
Autumn: mild, cooling days and quiet roads, with more rain.
Spring: changeable, showery weather and lambs in the fields.

risks.note: Ex-tropical cyclones can bring flooding and closed roads to Northland, the Coromandel and Hawke's Bay.
Winter storms with flooding and slips on rural roads.

recurringHolidays.name: New Zealand summer holidays
recurringHolidays.effect: Campsites, Great Walk huts, Cook Strait ferries and rental cars book out; prices peak.

recurringHolidays.name: Easter
recurringHolidays.effect: A long weekend with busy roads and full holiday towns.

prices.notes: Campervans are the classic way to travel, but rental prices double over Christmas–January. The Tongariro Crossing shuttle costs about NZ$50–80.

regions.name: South Island
regions.description: Christchurch, Kaikōura, Marlborough and Abel Tasman, the West Coast and the Franz Josef and Fox glaciers, Aoraki/Mount Cook and Lake Tekapo, Queenstown, Wānaka, Fiordland (Milford and Doubtful sounds) and Dunedin; climate figures are for Queenstown.

best.why: Late summer and autumn: settled 18–22 °C days, Great Walks open, golden poplars around Queenstown and Arrowtown in April and the summer crowds gone.
Ski season: reliable snow at Coronet Peak, The Remarkables, Cardrona and Treble Cone, with crisp, clear alpine days.

worst.why: The gap between seasons: cold, short days, Great Walks out of season and the ski lifts not yet open, with snow and avalanche risk on the Milford Road.

shoulder.why: Peak summer: long days and warm weather, but full huts, campsites and Milford cruises, sandflies and the year's highest prices.
Late autumn colours and frosty mornings.
Spring: snow melting, waterfalls in full flow and changeable weather; Milford Road avalanche risk until November.

risks.note: Fiordland and the West Coast get 6–7 m of rain a year; flights, cruises and glacier helicopter trips are often cancelled.
The Milford Road (SH94) closes at times for avalanche control.
Snow closes alpine passes (Lewis, Arthur's, Haast) and chains may be required.

recurringHolidays.name: Winter school holidays
recurringHolidays.effect: Queenstown and Wānaka ski fields are at their busiest and lodging prices peak.

recurringHolidays.name: New Zealand summer holidays
recurringHolidays.effect: Campsites, Great Walk huts, Cook Strait ferries and rental cars book out; prices peak.

recurringHolidays.name: Easter
recurringHolidays.effect: A long weekend with busy roads and full holiday towns.

prices.notes: Queenstown is the most expensive place in the country, especially in January and July. Great Walk huts cost about NZ$70–100 a night in season and must be booked months ahead.

countries.name: Palau
countries.summary: Palau is hot and humid all year (around 31 °C) with rain in every month, but there is a drier season from about January to April, when the trade winds bring calmer seas and the best conditions for diving Blue Corner, German Channel and the Rock Islands. June to October is the wettest period, with south-west monsoon winds that roughen the sea; Palau is usually south of the main typhoon tracks but can be hit. Chinese New Year and East Asian holidays bring tour groups from Taiwan, Korea and Japan.
countries.splitReason: Koror, the Rock Islands, Babeldaob and Peleliu are close together and share one climate.

regions.name: Whole country
regions.description: Koror, the Rock Islands Southern Lagoon (Milky Way, Jellyfish Lake), the dive sites of Blue Corner and German Channel, Babeldaob, Peleliu and Kayangel.

best.why: Dry season: calm seas, less rain and excellent visibility for diving, snorkelling and kayaking among the Rock Islands.

worst.why: Wettest months with south-west monsoon winds, rough crossings to the outer dive sites and a typhoon risk.

shoulder.why: Rains increasing, still decent diving.
Rain easing; good diving between showers.

risks.note: Typhoons usually pass to the north but occasionally strike (Haiyan in 2013, Bopha in 2012).
Monsoon winds make boat rides to the outer reefs rough.

recurringHolidays.name: Chinese New Year
recurringHolidays.effect: Tour groups from Taiwan and China fill Koror's hotels and dive boats.

prices.notes: All visitors pay a $100 Pristine Paradise environmental fee, plus a Rock Islands permit (about $50) for diving and kayaking. Two-tank boat dives cost about $150–200.

countries.name: Papua New Guinea
aliases: Independent State of Papua New Guinea
countries.summary: Papua New Guinea is hot and humid on the coasts all year, with cooler days in the Highlands. Most of the country has a wetter season from December to March and a drier season from May to October, which is the time for trekking the Kokoda Track, travelling in the Highlands and the big cultural shows: the Mount Hagen Show in mid-August and the Goroka Show around Independence Day in mid-September. Diving at Kimbe Bay, Milne Bay and Kavieng is good for most of the year outside the stormiest months. Infrastructure is limited and crime is a real concern in Port Moresby, Lae and parts of the Highlands, so check government travel advice and travel with a reputable operator.
countries.splitReason: Visitors combine Port Moresby, the Highlands, the Sepik and the islands, which share the same broad May–October dry season; local exceptions such as Lae and Alotau are noted rather than split.

regions.name: Whole country
regions.description: Port Moresby, the Kokoda Track, the Highlands (Mount Hagen, Goroka, Tari), the Sepik River, Madang, Rabaul and East New Britain, Kimbe Bay, Alotau and Milne Bay, Kavieng and the Trobriand Islands.

best.why: Drier season: fewer downpours, passable Highlands roads and Kokoda conditions, and the Mount Hagen (August) and Goroka (September) shows.

worst.why: Wet season: heavy daily rain, landslides on the Highlands Highway, muddy, dangerous Kokoda conditions and cancelled flights.

shoulder.why: Rains easing; Kokoda trekking season begins.
Heat and humidity building with the first storms; good diving in calm seas.

risks.note: Flooding and cancelled domestic flights, worst in Lae and the Highlands.
Slips close the Highlands Highway and remote roads.
Frequent earthquakes; Rabaul's Tavurvur and other volcanoes are active.

recurringHolidays.name: Mount Hagen Cultural Show
recurringHolidays.effect: Hundreds of Highlands sing-sing groups gather; flights and the few hotels in Mount Hagen book out months ahead.

recurringHolidays.name: Goroka Show
recurringHolidays.effect: PNG's largest cultural show; Goroka accommodation books out and flights fill.

prices.notes: Hotels are scarce and expensive, and most visitors use organised tours or lodges with transfers. Kokoda treks cost about $2,500–4,000 with a licensed operator.

countries.name: Samoa
countries.summary: Samoa is hot and humid all year (around 29–30 °C). The drier season from May to October brings more sunshine, lower humidity and calmer seas, and is the best time for the beaches of Upolu and Savai'i; the Teuila Festival in early September is a highlight. November to April is the wet season, with heavy tropical downpours and a cyclone risk that peaks from December to March. Christmas and New Year bring many Samoans home from New Zealand and Australia, filling flights.
countries.splitReason: Upolu and Savai'i are small, close together and share one tropical climate, with the wetter season the same on both islands.

regions.name: Whole country
regions.description: Apia and Upolu (Lalomanu Beach, To Sua Ocean Trench), Manono and Savai'i with its lava fields, blowholes and beach fales.

best.why: Drier season: sunny 29 °C days, lower humidity, calm lagoons for snorkelling and the Teuila Festival in September.

worst.why: Peak of the wet season: heavy downpours, oppressive humidity and the main cyclone risk.

shoulder.why: Rains building and humidity rising.
Wet season easing, quiet and green.

risks.note: Tropical cyclones, most likely December to March.
Flash flooding in Apia and on coastal roads.

recurringHolidays.name: Teuila Festival
recurringHolidays.effect: Samoa's national cultural festival in Apia, with fire-knife dancing and fautasi boat races; Apia hotels fill.

recurringHolidays.name: Christmas and New Year
recurringHolidays.effect: Flights from New Zealand and Australia fill with returning Samoans and fares rise.

prices.notes: Open-sided beach fales with breakfast and dinner cost about $40–70 per person. Sundays are for church and family: most shops and many activities close.

countries.name: Solomon Islands
countries.summary: The Solomon Islands are hot and humid all year (around 30 °C), with rain in every month. The south-east trade-wind season from May to October is drier, breezier and the best time for diving the Second World War wrecks off Guadalcanal and the lagoons of the Western Province. December to April is wetter, with heavy downpours and a cyclone risk. Tourism is small-scale, so book lodges and the infrequent domestic flights ahead.
countries.splitReason: Guadalcanal, the Western Province and Malaita share one tropical climate with a drier mid-year season; tourism is small-scale, with no regional differences that change when to go.

regions.name: Whole country
regions.description: Honiara and the Guadalcanal battlefields and wrecks, Gizo and Munda in the Western Province, Marovo Lagoon, Tulagi, Malaita and Tetepare.

best.why: Trade-wind season: fewer heavy showers, steady breezes and the best visibility for diving the wartime wrecks and Marovo Lagoon.

worst.why: The wettest months, with daily downpours, high humidity and the peak cyclone risk.

shoulder.why: Hot and humid as the rains return.
Rain easing, seas calming.

risks.note: Tropical cyclones can cut flights and boat links.
An active seismic zone with occasional tsunami warnings.

prices.notes: Honiara hotels are expensive for their standard; village eco-lodges in the Western Province cost $40–80 with meals. Malaria is present, so take prophylaxis.

countries.name: Tonga
countries.summary: Tonga lies further south than most Pacific islands, so its dry season (May to October) is pleasantly cool at 24–26 °C. Humpback whales come to Vava'u and Ha'apai to calve from July to October, when Tonga is one of the few places where you can swim with them. November to April is hot, humid and wet, with a significant cyclone risk from December to March. The Heilala Festival in early July is the main national celebration.
countries.splitReason: Tongatapu, Ha'apai and Vava'u share the same seasons; the whale season and the wet season are the same across the island groups.

regions.name: Whole country
regions.description: Nuku'alofa and Tongatapu, the Vava'u group (Neiafu, the sailing anchorages), the low coral islands of Ha'apai and the hiking island of 'Eua.

best.why: Whale season in the dry months: swimming with humpbacks in Vava'u and Ha'apai, steady trade winds for sailing and comfortable 24–26 °C days.

worst.why: Hot, humid wet season with heavy downpours and the peak cyclone risk (Cyclone Gita hit Tongatapu in February 2018).

shoulder.why: Dry season starting, cooler and calm, but the whales have not yet arrived.
Warming up with more showers; the last whales leave in early November.

risks.note: Tropical cyclones, most likely December to March.
An active seismic zone; the 2022 Hunga Tonga eruption caused a damaging tsunami.

recurringHolidays.name: Heilala Festival
recurringHolidays.effect: Tonga's main festival, around the King's birthday, with parades and a beauty pageant; Nuku'alofa hotels fill.

prices.notes: A whale-swim trip costs about $150–250 a day and should be booked well ahead for August and September. Sunday is a strict day of rest: no flights, shops or tours.

countries.name: Tuvalu
countries.summary: Tuvalu is a chain of low atolls just south of the equator, hot and humid all year (around 30 °C) with rain in every month. The south-east trade-wind season from May to October is slightly drier and breezier, which makes it the most comfortable time to visit. November to April is wetter, with westerly storms, the occasional cyclone and king tides that flood parts of Funafuti in February and March. Flights from Suva run only a few times a week.
countries.splitReason: Funafuti and the outer atolls are tiny and share one equatorial climate; nearly all visitors stay on Funafuti.

regions.name: Whole country
regions.description: Funafuti atoll (Fongafale, the lagoon and the Funafuti Conservation Area) and the outer atolls reached by government ship.

best.why: Trade-wind season: slightly less rain, steady breezes and calmer, clearer water for snorkelling in the Funafuti Conservation Area.

worst.why: Wettest months, with westerly gales, cyclone risk and king tides flooding low ground on Funafuti.

shoulder.why: Rains easing.
Showers increasing as the westerly season begins.

risks.note: King tides push seawater up through the ground on Funafuti.
Occasional tropical cyclones and westerly gales.

prices.notes: Prices are in Australian dollars. There are only a few guesthouses and one hotel on Funafuti; book flights and rooms together.

countries.name: Vanuatu
countries.summary: Vanuatu is warm all year, with a cooler, drier season from May to October (24–27 °C) and a hot, humid wet season from November to April when cyclones are a real risk. The dry season is the best time for Mount Yasur volcano on Tanna, diving the SS President Coolidge off Santo and the beaches of Efate. The Naghol land-diving ceremony on Pentecost is held on Saturdays from April to early June. Australian and New Zealand school holidays bring families to Port Vila's resorts.
countries.splitReason: Efate, Santo, Tanna and the outer islands share the same tropical wet and dry seasons, with the north (Santo) slightly wetter.

regions.name: Whole country
regions.description: Port Vila and Efate, Espiritu Santo (Champagne Beach, the President Coolidge wreck), Tanna and Mount Yasur, Pentecost, Malekula and Ambrym.

best.why: Dry season: 24–27 °C days, low humidity, calm seas for diving and clear evenings at the rim of Mount Yasur.

worst.why: Wettest months with steamy heat, frequent downpours and the peak cyclone risk (Cyclone Pam devastated the islands in March 2015).

shoulder.why: Hot, humid and increasingly showery; cyclone season begins.
Rains easing and land-diving season starting on Pentecost.

risks.note: Severe tropical cyclones can close airports and cut inter-island links.
Yasur, Ambrym and other volcanoes are active; access is closed when alert levels rise.
Frequent earthquakes with occasional tsunami warnings.

recurringHolidays.name: Naghol (land diving), Pentecost
recurringHolidays.effect: The original bungee jump, timed to the yam harvest; tours from Port Vila and Santo book out.

recurringHolidays.name: Australian and New Zealand winter school holidays
recurringHolidays.effect: Port Vila's resorts fill with families.

prices.notes: Prices are quoted in vatu and are high because most goods are imported. A Mount Yasur trip from Port Vila (flights, transfers and park fee) costs $500 or more.
